finding.claim: update_doc overwrites a document body for any authenticated user; the can_edit result on line 19 is discarded, so no ownership or editor check gates the write.
finding.source: Authenticated user with any account who knows or can guess a doc_id; PUT /doc/<id> with JSON body {"body": ...}.

trace.note: can_edit(g.user, doc) called; return value discarded, no effect

finding.guards_checked: can_edit (docs.py:7-8) computed but not enforced; no require_edit/abort before write; no decorator, before_request hook, or ownership check in this file; g.user set by unseen middleware (if unset, AttributeError at line 19, a 500, not a bypass); contrast update_title (docs.py:24-29) which calls require_edit and returns 403 before mutating and is not affected.

verdict.guard_found: none effective. can_edit (docs.py:7-8) is called at docs.py:19 as a bare statement, so its bool result is discarded. No require_edit call, abort, or before_request hook precedes the write at docs.py:20. require_edit (docs.py:11-13) is only used by update_title (docs.py:27), not update_doc. The only other file in the directory is docs.py, so nothing in-tree enforces auth on this route.
verdict.reason: docs.py:19 calls can_edit(g.user, doc) as a bare statement whose bool is discarded, so docs.py:20 overwrites doc["body"] for any user who reaches the route, while the sibling update_title at docs.py:27 correctly calls require_edit. The attacker only needs a valid session (g.user must be set by middleware not present here; if unset it is a 500 at line 19, not a bypass), and the write is not blocked by any control I could find in the code available.
